events.event: Japan public holiday: Mountain Day, markets closed
events.description: Japan's stock, bond and money markets are shut for the Mountain Day public holiday. Liquidity in yen crosses is typically thinner than usual through the Tokyo session as a result, which can exaggerate price moves on any other news that lands today.

The British Retail Consortium's monthly tracker of like for like store and online spending, released ahead of the official ONS retail sales figures. An early, partial read on UK consumer demand that can move sterling at the margin if it diverges sharply from recent trend.

A privately run monthly survey of large Japanese manufacturers that acts as an early, unofficial preview of the Bank of Japan's own quarterly Tankan survey. Useful for gauging shifts in corporate sentiment between the official releases, though it typically has limited standalone impact on the yen.

events.event: Japan money supply, M2 and M3 (July)
events.description: The Bank of Japan's monthly measures of broad money circulating in the economy. A slow moving indicator that rarely surprises markets on its own, but forms part of the backdrop economists use to judge whether the BoJ's policy stance is loosening or tightening financial conditions.

events.revisedNote: The June reading has been corrected to -6; it was carried as -5 in the last update. National Australia Bank's July survey has since printed unchanged at -6.
events.description: National Australia Bank's monthly survey of business sentiment and conditions. Released the day before the RBA's decision, it is watched closely for any last minute shift in the domestic backdrop that could tilt the Board's language.

events.event: RBA interest rate decision and Statement on Monetary Policy
events.description: The Reserve Bank's Monetary Policy Board decision, released alongside the quarterly Statement on Monetary Policy that carries the Bank's updated growth and inflation forecasts. The Board held the cash rate at 4.35% for a second straight meeting, a unanimous and widely expected decision after June's CPI came in below expectations. The RBA signalled inflation could stay above target until mid 2027 and said it would raise rates further if needed, so the accompanying statement's tone mattered as much as the decision itself.

Governor Michele Bullock's press conference following the rate decision. She said the economy was slowing as expected but that the Board would do what is necessary to bring inflation back to its 2 to 3 percent target, including raising the cash rate further if upside risks materialise, a message markets read as keeping a hike on the table despite today's hold.

events.event: South Africa Quarterly Labour Force Survey (Q2)
events.description: Stats SA's quarterly survey of employment and unemployment, one of the most closely watched domestic releases for the rand given South Africa's persistently high jobless rate. The Q1 reading marked a jump to 32.7%, so this update is watched for whether the labour market weakness has continued into the second quarter.

events.revisedNote: A consensus estimate of 97.5 has now been published for this release; none was available in the last update.
events.description: The National Federation of Independent Business's monthly survey of small business sentiment on hiring, sales and pricing plans, usually released on the second Tuesday of the month. A useful cross check on the health of Main Street businesses, though typically a secondary mover for the dollar.

events.event: German Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices, final (July)
events.description: The final, confirmed reading of Germany's HICP inflation figure, the measure used for comparison across the euro area and a key input into the ECB's policy thinking. It rarely diverges from the flash estimate, but as the bloc's largest economy, any surprise revision can move the euro at the margin.

Statistics Canada's forward looking measure of planned construction activity, based on permits issued by municipalities. A useful, if volatile, early signal for the housing sensitive parts of the Canadian growth outlook.

events.consensus: +3.4% y/y headline, +2.5% y/y core, both a touch cooler than June
events.description: The Bureau of Labor Statistics' inflation report for July, due at 8.30am Eastern time (1.30pm UK time), is the most closely watched US release of the week. Headline CPI has been reaccelerating in recent months as the conflict driven jump in oil prices around the Strait of Hormuz feeds into energy costs, keeping the Fed under pressure to balance its inflation fight against signs of labour market cooling. Consensus looks for a slight cooling to 3.4% y/y headline and 2.5% y/y core, and after a weak and confusing July jobs report this print carries extra weight: a hot number would bolster the hawkish minority on the FOMC and complicate the case for a near term rate cut, while an in line or softer number would support the view that the Fed can look through the energy spike and prioritise the cooling labour market.

events.event: RBNZ Survey of Expectations: two year inflation expectations (Q3)
events.description: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand's quarterly survey of businesses and forecasters on where they expect inflation to sit two years out. Two year expectations climbed to 2.53% in the second quarter from 2.37% in the first, so this update is watched for whether that upward drift has continued, since a further rise would narrow the RBNZ's room to ease policy.

events.event: China money supply (M0, M1, M2), new yuan loans and Total Social Financing (July)
events.previous: new loans of RMB 1.61 trillion; outstanding loan growth of 5.2% y/y (June)
events.consensus: new loans seen roughly flat to modestly higher year on year at around RMB 50 billion, with outstanding loan growth easing slightly to about 5.1% y/y; TSF growth around 7.4% y/y
events.description: The People's Bank of China's monthly credit bundle, covering broad money supply growth, new bank lending and total social financing, the broadest gauge of credit flowing into the real economy. Usually published without a fixed hour, it is watched closely for whether Beijing's stimulus is gaining traction, with a weak reading pointing to soft domestic demand that carries knock on relevance for the Australian and New Zealand dollars given China's role as their top trading partner.

The Office for National Statistics' first estimate of UK economic growth for the second quarter, published alongside the June monthly GDP figure. GDP grew 0.6% in the first quarter and consensus looks for a slowdown to around 0.4% in the second, so this reading is the key gauge of whether momentum has eased as expected; a stronger than expected print is generally supportive for sterling, while a miss adds to the case for the Bank of England to keep policy accommodative.

events.event: UK trade balance, index of production and construction output (June)
events.description: Released alongside the GDP figures, this bundle covers the goods and services trade balance, manufacturing and industrial output, and construction sector activity for June. These are the underlying components that feed into the quarterly growth number and are watched for a more granular read on where UK momentum is coming from.

events.consensus: annual rate expected to ease from June's 5.5%, with some estimates near 5.1% or lower
events.description: The Bureau of Labor Statistics' measure of wholesale price pressures, released a day after CPI. June's headline PPI fell 0.3% on the month but was still up 5.5% on the year, and this report is watched for whether producer level inflation is cooling from that pace or if the energy driven price pressures seen in the consumer figures are also showing up further up the supply chain.

The Department of Labor's weekly count of new unemployment benefit claims, released alongside PPI. A high frequency, early read on the US labour market that typically has limited standalone impact but is watched closely for any signs of a sharper turn in hiring conditions following the weak and confusing July payrolls print.

The National Energy Administration's monthly tally of nationwide power usage, released without a fixed hour. A high frequency, real economy proxy for industrial activity that investors sometimes trust more than the official GDP figures, with relevance for the Australian and New Zealand dollars given trade linkages to Chinese factory demand.

events.event: US Retail Sales and Retail Sales Control Group (July)
events.description: The Census Bureau's monthly report on spending at US retailers, a leading indicator of consumer demand and a key input into the GDP outlook. The Control Group strips out volatile categories such as autos and gasoline and feeds directly into GDP calculations, so it is watched closely alongside the headline number; a soft print would add to the case for the Fed to look past sticky inflation and focus on a cooling consumer, while a strong one would complicate the argument for a near term rate cut.

Statistics Canada's monthly measure of factory sales, a timely gauge of demand for Canadian manufactured goods both at home and among export customers such as the US. A secondary release that offers a useful, if volatile, cross check on the health of Canada's industrial sector.

events.event: University of Michigan Consumer Sentiment Index, preliminary (August)
events.description: The University of Michigan's early read on US household confidence, covering current conditions and expectations for the economy, jobs and inflation. Sentiment has been unusually weak and volatile through 2026, and the survey's inflation expectations components are watched almost as closely as the headline index for what they imply about the Fed's inflation fight.

The Cabinet Office's first estimate of Japanese growth for the second quarter, due at 8.50am Tokyo time (12.50am UK time). First quarter growth was revised down to 1.8% annualised on weaker capital spending, and economists expect a further quarter of solid, if unspectacular, expansion of around 2.0%. The number feeds directly into the debate over how much room the Bank of Japan has to keep normalising policy, so a strong beat would support a firmer yen while a miss would push back expectations for further BoJ tightening.

Statistics Canada's headline inflation report for July, the top domestic release of the week for the Canadian dollar. Annual inflation cooled to 2.8% in June from 3.2% in May as gasoline price gains slowed, with the core CPI trim and CPI median measures both dipping below the Bank of Canada's 2% target. This report is watched closely for whether that cooling trend continued into July, shaping expectations for the Bank of Canada's next policy move.

The Federal Reserve Bank of New York's monthly gauge of manufacturing activity in its district, one of the earliest regional Fed surveys each month and a useful early signal for the national ISM manufacturing report. July's reading jumped to 15.6 from 5.7 in June, comfortably beating forecasts, so this update is watched for whether that strength has been sustained into August.

The National Association of Home Builders' monthly gauge of builder confidence in the market for newly built single family homes, based on a survey of current sales conditions, sales expectations and buyer traffic. Sentiment has stayed below the neutral 50 level for well over a year on affordability concerns, and this update is watched as an early signal ahead of the following day's housing starts data.
